title: "Tax Evasion and Productivity: Identifying and Correcting for Cost Overreporting"
jmp: true
draft: false
author:
  - name: Hans Martinez

date: today
abstract: |
  Sales and value-added taxes that credit purchases reward firms for overreporting their inputs: every fictitious dollar of deductible inputs lowers their tax liability, and thus the higher the rate, the larger the reward. However, how this evasion responds to the tax rate is largely unknown, because true inputs are not observed and firms that overreport may be mistaken for low-productivity firms. I separate overreporting from productivity using the production function, with corporations, which government and market scrutiny keep from evading, as the truth-reporting benchmark. My approach does not require confidential tax records and applies equally to standard firm-level surveys and administrative data. I apply it to Colombian manufacturing firms from 1981 to 1991, a period that includes a 1983 reform that raised the sales-tax rate in most industries. After the reform, overreporting by unincorporated firms in the affected industries, measured as a share of true materials, rose, and by 1987 it reached about 9%. I then estimate a structural model of detection and evasion costs, and find that a 0.5% increase in the sales-tax rate raises claimed deductions by between 16% and 28%, far more than its mechanical effect, while cuts lower them only gradually: the smallest cut statistically distinguishable from current policy is 8%. The approach also yields a statistical test, valid for any detection probability, evasion cost and common technology, whose rejections can only point to overreporting. The test detects overreporting in 9 of 20 industries, including four of the five largest. Among the five industries where the test rejects the absence of overreporting at the 1% level, firms overreport on average between 11% and 25% of their true materials. Finally, correcting for overreporting yields consistently smaller output elasticities of materials and less dispersed productivity, with a 90–10 ratio about 40% lower and a half-life of productivity shocks two to seven times longer.
thanks: |
